title: Snowmass Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Snowmass wells have a median depth of 86 feet, with typical finished-well costs modeled at $11,600-$20,600.
h1: Snowmass, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Water-well records around Snowmass show a mountain setting where many wells are relatively shallow, but fractured bedrock can still make site conditions unpredictable. The median recorded depth is 86 feet, and the middle half runs from 54 to 160 feet. Most wells are domestic or household wells, and the reported median yield is 15.0 gallons per minute.

These figures come from Colorado DWR permit records within five miles of Snowmass in Pitkin County. They are useful for comparing nearby properties and planning a drilling budget, but they do not guarantee what a new well will produce. Review the actual neighboring wells, water rights, septic limits, and building plans before buying land.

sections.heading: Snowmass well depth: shallow records, hard-rock variability
sections.html:
Snowmass wells have a recorded median depth of 86 feet. The middle half is between 54 and 160 feet, while the ninetieth percentile reaches 300 feet. The deepest well in the records is 758 feet. That spread matters when a driller prepares a bid: a typical estimate may fit a shallow hole, but a difficult fractured-bedrock site can require substantially more drilling.

Of the recorded wells, 56% are under 100 feet, 34% are between 100 and 300 feet, and 10% are between 300 and 600 feet. Only 1% are deeper than 600 feet. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with far fewer wells in Mancos or alluvial aquifers.

sections.heading: How much water can a Snowmass well produce?
sections.html:
The reported median well yield near Snowmass is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 70% of wells with yield information report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 26% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Only 3% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and none are recorded below 1 gallon per minute.

That is a strong local record, but the yield sample includes only 296 wells, not every permit. A good reported yield does not remove the need for a pump test, storage planning, and confirmation that the permitted use fits the home, livestock, irrigation, or other proposed demand. Household-use wells still have Colorado water-right and permit requirements.

sections.heading: Snowmass water levels and the recent reading
sections.html:
Among the 75 wells reporting a static water level, the median depth to water is 38 feet. The middle half is from 18 to 67 feet below the surface. That is useful when estimating pump placement and initial site work, but water levels can vary with location, season, weather, pumping, and the local fracture network.

The decade series shows median readings of 25 feet in the 1990s, 26 feet in the 2010s, and 43 feet in the 2020s. The newer measurements are therefore deeper, which may indicate a change in measured water levels, but the sample is limited and does not prove a basin-wide declining water table. Ask for the original well logs and recent measurements for the specific property.

sections.heading: Snowmass permit history and the drillers in the records
sections.html:
Permit activity was highest in the 1990s, with 329 permits, followed by 267 in the 2000s. The records include 121 permits from the 2010s and 79 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Across the search area, DWR records contain 1,280 wells, with 625 recorded as constructed and 760 reporting a total depth.

The most active names in these records are Shelton Drilling Corporation, with 412 wells; Collins Drilling Co, listed as Collins, F. E. “Bodie,” with 151; and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc., listed as Shelton, Steve, with 115. These counts describe permit history, not current availability or a recommendation. Confirm licensing, insurance, scope, and the conditions included in any current proposal.

sections.heading: What a new Snowmass well may cost
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The modeled drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the median depth of 86 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $5,600 to $8,600. A finished well, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is modeled at about $11,600 to $20,600.

Those figures are planning numbers, not a guaranteed quote. The deepest local record is 758 feet, so depth risk can be significant even though most recorded wells are shallower. Ask a driller to separate drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, electrical work, trenching, water testing, and permits. A bid should also explain what happens if the hole is dry or the first water-bearing fracture does not provide an acceptable yield.

sections.heading: Snowmass water-quality, septic, and building checks
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information within about ten miles includes 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 historic mine feature. There are no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the mapped facts. These locations do not establish contamination at a particular parcel, but they are a reason to test the well rather than assume mountain water is automatically safe.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured granite or gneiss even when nearby wells perform well. Before building, confirm the well permit, production test, static level, casing and grout details, and laboratory water results. Check the proposed septic area separately: soil, slope, setbacks, reserve-area requirements, and available room for the house, driveway, and utility trenches can control what can actually be built.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Woody Creek and Snowmass
sections.html:
Use the records from Snowmass, Woody Creek, Basalt, Snowmass Village, El Jebel, Aspen, and Catherine as a starting point for local comparisons, while giving the closest wells the most weight. The database has 1,280 permits, but only 296 report a pump yield and 75 report a static water level. Missing data is not proof of a problem, but it means a buyer should obtain the original documents instead of relying on a map summary.

For an existing home, verify the permit, well construction report, pump test, water quality, storage, and actual household performance. For vacant land, make the well and septic investigations part of due diligence before closing. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be necessary for some uses. A Colorado DWR review can clarify the permit and water-right restrictions before you commit to a building design.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Snowmass, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within five miles of Snowmass is 86 feet. The middle half runs from 54 to 160 feet, but the ninetieth percentile reaches 300 feet and the deepest record is 758 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss create local variability, so nearby well logs are more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Snowmass?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 86-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $5,600 to $8,600. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $11,600 to $20,600. A difficult site or deeper hole can cost more.

faq.q: How much water does a Snowmass well produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Seventy percent of wells with yield data report more than 15 gallons per minute. The yield sample includes 296 wells, so a buyer should still review the specific well test and confirm that production meets the planned use.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Snowmass?
faq.a: The permit map does not prove that any individual well is safe or unsafe to drink. Within about ten miles, records show 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 historic mine feature, with no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory and repeat testing when conditions or ownership change.

faq.q: Are Snowmass wells getting deeper or running lower?
faq.a: Reported median static water levels were 25 feet below the surface in the 1990s, 26 feet in the 2010s, and 43 feet in the 2020s. The newer readings are deeper, but only 75 wells report static water levels, so this does not establish a basin-wide decline. Obtain recent measurements and the original logs for the property you are evaluating.
